summary: SIP back-to-back user agents can cause endless request loops because they generate new requests with fresh Max-Forwards values. This document discusses why loop detection is difficult for these devices and sets out requirements for them to prevent infinite loops.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine passing a note around a circle where each person writes a new note and passes it on forever. This RFC explains how phone-call relays should notice that and stop.

questions: why do sip loops happen with b2bua
subtitle: SIP back-to-back user agents must copy and decrement Max-Forwards so request loops cannot run forever.

tldr.problem: SIP back-to-back user agents (B2BUAs) can reset Max-Forwards on the requests they generate, so a misconfiguration can become an unending routing loop.
tldr.mechanism: All B2BUA types MUST copy and decrement Max-Forwards, and copy Max-Breadth, like a proxy, and Via-based loop detection is RECOMMENDED.
tldr.outcome: Loops are bounded by the hop limit, but B2BUAs that hide hop counts for privacy have to choose between obfuscation and loop protection.

today: RFC 7332 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why B2BUAs Loop Forever
sections.content:
RFC 3261 prevents infinite forwarding loops, and RFC 5393 mitigates parallel forking amplification, but neither normatively defines behavior for B2BUAs. Because a B2BUA is a User Agent Client on one side, it may legally build new requests with a new Max-Forwards value. The RFC says unbounded SIP request loops have actually occurred numerous times, usually from misconfiguration, and have caused service outages and hard troubleshooting.

Most B2BUA types can also create the UAC-side request without copying the Via headers, which stops Via-based loop detection from working earlier than the Max-Forwards limit. Vendor workarounds, such as counting requests per caller and called URI pair, are called brittle and prone to error. The last defense is to limit hops with Max-Forwards.
sections.plainLanguage: Each relay starts a brand new note, so nobody notices the note keeps coming back. Counting hops is the one reliable fix.

sections.title: Loop Detection and Max-Forwards Rules
sections.content:
B2BUAs are RECOMMENDED to implement the Via loop-detection mechanism defined for a proxy in RFC 5393.

All B2BUA types MUST copy the received Max-Forwards header field from the request on their UAS side to any request they generate on the UAC side, and decrement it as a proxy would under RFC 3261. As a UAS, a B2BUA MUST also check the received value and reject or respond to the request if it is zero. If the request had no Max-Forwards, one MUST be created, and its value SHOULD be 70.

This applies to dialog-forming and out-of-dialog requests. B2BUAs MAY do the same for in-dialog requests, though that may cause issues with devices that set Max-Forwards from the number of Via or Record-Route headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the countdown going from one relay to the next, and stop when it hits zero. If there was no countdown, start one at 70.

sections.title: Max-Breadth Rules
sections.content:
All B2BUA types MUST copy the received Max-Breadth header field to any requests they generate on the UAC side, as a proxy would under RFC 5393. They MUST follow the proxy requirements in Section 5.3.3 of RFC 5393, including generating the header if none is received and limiting its maximum value.

B2BUAs that send parallel requests for a single incoming request MUST also follow the Max-Breadth rules as if they were a parallel forking proxy. Otherwise the parallel forking amplification protection in RFC 5393 is defeated.
sections.plainLanguage: The same idea applies to how many copies of a note may be sent out at once: relays must keep that limit too.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Trade-off
sections.content:
The document adds no issues beyond those in Section 7 of RFC 5393. Some B2BUAs reset Max-Forwards and Max-Breadth to hide how many hops a request has traversed, for privacy or security. That goal is at odds with this document, and administrators can decide whether obfuscation or loop detection matters more.

Manufacturers MUST comply with the rules by default, but MAY provide user-configurable overrides.
sections.plainLanguage: Some relays hide the hop count to keep it private. The rules are on by default, but an owner may switch them off.
